headline: Regulatory pressure will hit smaller private credit funds with lax lending policies; larger players already have risk management layers in place and can manage distressed loan books through to completion given supply shortages
reasoning: Ashley Tilston notes that incoming regulatory scrutiny on private credit will disproportionately affect smaller funds with weaker lending policies, while larger players like Balmain Private already have risk management infrastructure. Balmain Private has taken over distressed projects and is managing them through to completion before on-selling, which is feasible given the lack of housing supply. The lack of supply means patient capital can work through problem loans, though some lenders will still face pain from poor underwriting. The broader point is that quality of execution varies across the sector as it does in any investment class.
quote: Yeah, there will be. And I think that's going to capture sort of like the smaller funds who have got sort of LAX lending policies, but sort of the big end of town have already got those sort of like those like layers in place or the ability to be able to sort of manage our projects. So I know that the head of Balmain Private came out today and gave an interview talking about how they're handling the particular their exposure to the loan book. They have just taken over the sides and then we'll send them through to completion. Now what that requires is for them to then on sell those properties. But again, we have a lack of supply in the marketplace. So as long as you have time on your side, you should be able to get through. That's not to say there aren't going to be lenders out there who have got exposure in a way that is going to cause a pain. But that's like that with any investment, any any investment we go into, there's going to be people who do the right thing and people who had to do the wrong thing.

headline: Negative gearing grandfathering is prompting a structural shift: clients refinancing to 10-year interest-only loans and unlocking property equity to redeploy into equities rather than buying more investment properties
reasoning: Budget changes have created a two-tier property investment landscape. Clients who are grandfathered under existing negative gearing rules have little incentive to repay principal, driving a surge in 10-year interest-only loan refinancing now offered by several banks. With new investment property purchases increasingly impractical — particularly new builds — clients are instead unlocking equity from existing properties and deploying that capital into the stock market. Ashley Tilston frames this as a structural pivot in how his client base builds wealth, moving away from the traditional buy-leverage-repeat property strategy.
quote: Some of the banks have actually moved to introduce 10 year interest only loans. And so the conversation is coming up with clients around, well, if your property is exempt, you've got an existing property, you your you know, your grandfathered in for negative gearing doesn't make any sense for you to actually repay that debt. And so we've seen this huge surge in interest in actually clients calling up and saying, Hey, my broker is told for me, I can get 10 year interest only loans and people are actually going to market to refinance... clients are using to look the equity, use the equity in the property, unlock that and then try and find different investment opportunities, mainly the stock market.
episode_title: Ashley's take on the super-for-housing push | the advisory

headline: Proposal to redirect 3% of compulsory super to mortgage or rental costs is poor economics: the maths only work if the home loan rate exceeds the super fund's compounded return, and diverting super to rent would simply inflate rents further
reasoning: Ashley Tilston argues that the proposed policy to redirect 3% of compulsory superannuation toward mortgage or rental costs does not stack up numerically. For the maths to work, the interest rate on a home loan would need to exceed the compounded return of the super fund, which is unlikely over the long term. Diverting super contributions to rent would simply give landlords more scope to raise rents, leaving renters no better off. She characterises the proposal as good politics but bad economics, designed to attract attention on cost-of-living without rigorous modelling behind it.
quote: I heard this last night and I was driving in the car and I was like, OK, you know, on face value, it's a really, really good political manoeuvre to sort of like tackle cost of living. And my, my question to myself and my team this morning was, does this actually make sense? And the truth is the numbers don't stack up. I know that on the news last night, I think sort of Barnaby Joyce was grilled by, by the 7:30 report in relation to it. And there's no modelling done. It's look for the math to this to work, what you would have to have happen is that the the interest rate of your home loan would need to be higher than the compounded rate of the Super fund. On the same time, if you just divert money from super to pay rent, that's just going to remain that people will increase their rents. Look, All in all, it's not a good economic idea, but I can say it's probably a good political one because it's sort of, yeah, gives them attention that they are looking for.
episode_title: Ashley's take on the super-for-housing push | the advisory

headline: Selective but firm believer: private credit solves a real funding gap for development, backed by federal housing accord and state rezoning mandates, but fund quality varies sharply
reasoning: Ashley Tilston holds private credit exposure in client portfolios and remains a believer in the asset class. The investment thesis rests on the structural funding gap for residential development, supported by the federal housing accord target of 1.2 million properties over five years and state-level rezoning across major metropolitan cities. However, he cautions that not all private credit managers are equal and that liquidity risk (fund gating) is real; clients should only allocate capital they can afford to have illiquid. Increased regulatory scrutiny following the Baffler situation is seen as a positive for the sector, likely weeding out smaller funds with lax lending policies while larger, better-managed funds remain well-positioned.
quote: When it comes to private credit, people have to realise that it's not all the same thing. And this is where good fund managers and good credit managers will basically come to the fore. Nothing. There's nothing to be overly too scared about unless we have this massive rush in the marketplace at which particular point in time funds will gate, which means they'll stop redemptions. Now that can be very, very scary. But for a good diversified portfolio, clients who invest in this should only be allocating capital that they can be illiquid, that they don't need to access... One thing that's really interesting and why we're still a firm believer in it is that the problem that private credit is solving is the sort of the lack of funding for development. Now there's a government mandate both at a federal level to build what is it sort of the housing accord is 101.2 million properties over a five year. You then also have the rezoning which is occurring across major metropolitan cities by state governments, allowing for more development.
episode_title: Ashley's take on the super-for-housing push | the advisory

headline: Ashley Tilston warns Australian property investors must reassess return expectations as Treasury forecasts growth dropping from 6% to 2%
reasoning: Tilston notes that Treasury modelling points to future housing price growth of around 2% per annum, down from the 6% average seen over the past decade. This creates a fundamental disconnect between what property investors assumed they would earn and what they are likely to actually achieve. He argues investors need to treat property like any other investment and make rational decisions based on realistic future return assumptions rather than the old 'doubles every ten years' adage. He stresses this slowdown is intentional government policy, not a cyclical blip.
quote: if we're going by Treasury's modelling, if we've got a future, a forecasted growth rate of 2% as opposed to the 6% that we received on housing across Australia over the past decade, there's definitely going to be a disconnect between what people were assuming they were going to get out of their property investment and what they're actually going to achieve.
episode_title: Calling time on the property doubles every 10 years myth | the advisory

headline: Tilston challenges the 'property doubles every 10 years' myth, urging investors to reassess return expectations and compare property against share portfolios
reasoning: Tilston states the old adage that property doubles every ten years is no longer valid. He highlights hidden carry costs such as unexpected large strata bills and rising insurance premiums as risks that can erode returns. headline: Tilston highlights strata cost blowouts as a major hidden risk for both owner-occupiers and investors, particularly retirees
reasoning: Tilston provides real client examples where strata special levies have been far larger than anticipated — one client facing a $310,000 strata bill on a $1.4 million unit, another a retiree facing an $80,000 levy that materially erodes her retirement runway. He notes these costs are often buried in strata reports and overlooked, especially by first home buyers. Building inspection reports commissioned by selling agents may not adequately flag structural risks across entire buildings, and buyers can also overlook known issues when emotionally attached to a property.
quote: Real life story. I had two conversations with clients this week. Owner occupiers both strata one has a $310,000 strata bill on a 1.4 million unit purchase. The other has an $80,000 strata cost. So these are special levies being raised to do capital works in their homes. But she's a retiree. That's $80,000 means that she's got three years left on her runway. So we look at these through the perspective of, you know, it's an asset. But when you get close to retirement or you're in retirement, you can't afford these costs. This actually means that you can't go on that trip with your kids. So people have to start looking at this in a way that's more investment minded.

headline: Tilston urges property investors to treat holdings like equities and weigh total holding costs against realistic future capital growth
reasoning: Tilston argues that if capital growth has been compressed by policy to around 2%, the logical response would be to seek higher income (i.e. rent), but that this has real community consequences. He recommends investors be 'slightly agnostic' about their property and assess it as they would a share — asking whether the future value of the asset justifies all associated holding costs including interest, insurance, strata and taxes. The removal of negative gearing is also cited as a key cost consideration that changes the investment calculus.
quote: The logical thing would be I would try and increase the income side. But what we're really talking about is increasing rents. And that has a real tangible impact on the community. Everything is interconnected, and the important thing for property investors is to sort of take a take, a sort of step back and have a look at their individual property as an investment itself and slightly be agnostic to it. Think about it like you would. This is a share that I'm trading. A company that I purchased on the stock market. Is the future value of this asset going to be worthwhile holding, given all the costs and everything that we that comes along with property?

So what we've explored with certain clients is perhaps renovating your own home, reinvesting into your own home and adding value to it in the way of, say, a new bedroom or an expansion... if you renovate your home and you can grow the value of it, that's going to be a tax free gain.

headline: Negative gearing changes make residential investment property less attractive, pushing investors toward shares and super
reasoning: Ashley Tilston argues that with negative gearing now restricted on residential investment properties, investors with surplus capital need to find alternative vehicles. He notes the after-tax return is the key lens investors should use, and suggests shares and superannuation are now more compelling alternatives. He expresses a personal view that treating residential property and shares the same from a tax perspective is a mistake, and that encouraging more share investment would benefit the broader economy by funding businesses and wealth creation.
quote: If you've got surplus money. You can't buy a residential investment property and negatively gear. You want to be able to invest. This is a vehicle to do so, where you can reduce your alpha tax return by not having to pay the capital gains tax... I think it's a travesty that we're treating residential property and shares the same. If we had more people investing into shares, that would open up opportunities for countless other Australians to grow wealth, start businesses and the like.

headline: Investment bonds re-emerging as tax-efficient wealth vehicle post CGT changes given CGT-free status after 10 years
reasoning: Tilston highlights investment bonds as a revived strategy in the post-budget environment. These are tax-paid structures where tax is paid at the corporate rate of 30% within the bond, making them attractive for anyone on a marginal rate above 30%. Critically, after 10 years the investment becomes CGT-free, providing a pathway around the new minimum 30% CGT floor. While historically used for estate planning and children's education savings, they are now being positioned as a broader wealth-creation tool for investors who cannot access property with negative gearing or face higher tax burdens under the new rules.
quote: An investment bond sort of. It's a tax paid structure where you invest in this particular investment product. The tax is already paid for you. So it's paid a company tax rate of 30%. So it's really good for anybody who's on an income of higher than 30%. The catch with these investments though, is that over a period of time, after eight years, they start to become tax preference. And at the ten year mark, if you sell the investment, there's actually no further tax to pay. That means that they are CGT free. Now the we traditionally have used these for people who are retired, who can't put more money into superannuation... but now they're becoming much more of a targeted investment for people who want to continue to grow their wealth but want to try and sort of get around that minimum tax floor of 30% on capital gains tax, because, again, the payoff here is that at after ten years there are CGT free.
episode_title: Investing after the tax shake-up | the advisory

headline: Superannuation remains a key wealth-creation vehicle post CGT changes despite contribution caps
reasoning: Tilston identifies superannuation as a primary vehicle for wealth accumulation given the new tax environment. Contributions are capped at $32,500 for tax-deductible and $130,000 for non-concessional contributions this financial year, which limits its scalability, but it remains the most tax-efficient structure available for most Australians. quote: The key areas that we're continuing to look at is the family home. Maybe just invest more into the family home. But superannuation as a key vehicle to be able to grow wealth... contributions are capped at 32,500 for this year for a tax deductible contribution and $130,000 for another tax contribution. But people have to have the cash flow.

headline: Residential property investment appeal diminished post CGT changes as tax parity with equities removes key advantage
reasoning: Tilston notes that the natural pivot for investors away from property — moving into the stock market — is no longer as attractive because shares are now treated the same way from a tax perspective. The removal of preferential CGT treatment for residential investment property, combined with equivalent treatment of equities, has reduced the appeal of both asset classes relative to before. Clients are reassessing their entire wealth-generation strategy as a result.

The natural pivot that everyone has come to is like, I'll just invest into the stock market. But that's not no longer the case. They're getting treated the same and it's causing a lot of confusion.

headline: Tilston advocates for greater share investment as an alternative to residential property following tax changes, including via superannuation LRBA structures

The key appeal is that superannuation assets sold in retirement remain tax-free, making the after-tax return compelling. He sees this as an underused but legitimate path for clients to build wealth outside of residential property.
quote: There's a way that you can accelerate your your growth of your superannuation fund. Now you've got to it's a very complicated strategy, but it's something to very closely to take a look at for people who are looking to accelerate their wealth, because the end payoff of this is that superannuation is still tax free if you sell your assets in retirement. And so what you want to look at is what is that after tax return? And to be honest with you, it's really great that people would start to look more closely at investing in shares.

headline: CGT changes causing confusion among Australian investors as minimum 30% tax floor reshapes wealth-creation strategies beyond property
reasoning: Ashley Tilston from Spectrum Wealth Partners notes that the budget's capital gains tax changes — particularly the minimum 30% tax floor — are causing significant confusion among clients. While clients broadly accept changes to housing policy, they are uncertain about why the changes extend to shares and trusts. This is resetting how investors think about wealth creation, as the traditional pivot to the stock market is now less attractive given equities are treated similarly to property under the new rules.

What my clients are calling us about is they just don't understand why there are changes being done to shares, to trusts. And this is causing a great deal of confusion because clients, when you come and see a financial advisor, you're looking to create wealth.
